title: Beyond NISQ Assumptions: One-time Memory in the Classically Accessible Random-Oracle Model
authors: Boyang Chen, Tianren Liu, Luojian Wei
abstract: Quantum information enables many cryptographic primitives that are impossible in the classical world. A line of works has developed cryptographic protocol under the assumption that quantum adversaries are restricted to noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computing power, enabling strong one-time functionalities. But the advent of early fault-tolerant quantum computers eras will allow deeper logical quantum circuits, calling into questions the applicability of these NISQ-based assumptions.   In this work, we adapt the classically accessible random oracle model (CAROM) as in [BDF+11] and [AK22], in which adversaries are only allowed to classically query the random oracle. The restriction is well motivated for NISQ quantum adversaries and may remain plausible in the presence of early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Then, we show that an efficient simulation-secure one-time memory (OTM) is possible under CAROM. Our protocol uses only BB84 states and has quadratic communication: for a $λ$-bit message and integer-valued parameters $n=n(λ)$ and $\ell=\ell(λ)$, the construction uses $n\ell$ qubits and $(n+2)λ$ classical bits, and for any quantum adversary with at most $2^{\ell/2-1}-1$ classical queries to the random oracle, its simulation advantage is at most $(n+3)\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^n.$ Hence exponentially small simulation advantage in $n$.
summary: This paper develops a One-Time Memory (OTM) protocol secure in the Classically Accessible Random-Oracle Model (CAROM), addressing the limitations of NISQ-based security assumptions. By utilizing BB84 states and a structured oracle query mechanism, the authors achieve information-theoretic security with an exponentially small simulation advantage. This work advances the theoretical understanding of quantum cryptography for future fault-tolerant quantum computers.
main_problem: To construct an efficient One-Time Memory (OTM) protocol secure against quantum adversaries beyond the restrictive assumptions of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) computing.
main_result: The authors show that an efficient OTM scheme is possible under the Classically Accessible Random-Oracle Model (CAROM), achieving exponentially small simulation advantage for polynomial query bounds.
method: The protocol adapts the CAROM framework, using BB84 states and replacing basis information with oracle tags to ensure security against quantum adversaries.
model_or_system: The security proof is built within the abstract mathematical framework of the Classically Accessible Random-Oracle Model (CAROM), which restricts the adversary's interaction with the random oracle to classical queries.
key_observables: Simulation advantage (the probability of distinguishing the real protocol from the simulated one), communication complexity (qubits and classical bits).
important_parameters: Message length ($\lambda$), number of words ($n$), and word length ($\ell$), which are set as functions of $\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The security relies on the CAROM model, which is assumed to be more robust than NISQ assumptions, and the difficulty of coherently evaluating the random oracle.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, adapts the CAROM model, details the protocol construction using BB84 states and oracle tags, and culminates in a security proof that bounds the simulation advantage using techniques related to parallel repetition theorems.
why_interesting: While the paper is purely theoretical, its focus on robust cryptographic primitives and moving beyond NISQ assumptions is foundational for understanding the long-term computational limits of quantum information processing.
